issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile is not well aligned with the cognitive formulation. The only active edge is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from the selected appraisals. Overeating and busyness can follow from distressing appraisals, but 'Checking Surroundings' is a threat-monitoring/safety behavior that usually implies an active Threat component or a strong Trigger/Threat linkage, both of which are absent in the formulation and not represented elsewhere in the self-report.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm' is a global current-danger appraisal that typically pairs with a Threat presentation and supports behaviors like environmental scanning. But Threat is not represented as an active component in the formulation, and the rest of the negative appraisals are more about self-doubt and shattered assumptions. This makes the appraisal/strategy pattern clinically incoherent for the specified edge structure.

vignette:
Walter had been a delivery driver for forty years, and in all that time, he’d prided himself on knowing the city’s rhythms. He knew which streets to avoid at rush hour, which businesses had the friendliest receiving clerks, and which neighborhoods were safe at any time of day. That belief was shattered on a Tuesday afternoon in October. He was making a routine drop-off, a small parcel for a residential address, when a young man approached him on the porch. There was no warning, just a sudden, violent shove from behind that sent him sprawling, his head cracking against the concrete steps. The world went blurry and loud. He felt hands in his pockets, the sharp shame of his own helplessness, and the cold indifference in the young man’s eyes before he vanished down the street. The physical injuries were minor—a few stitches, a constellation of bruises—but the assault dismantled the world as Walter had known it.

In the months that followed, Walter came to believe that his own judgment was fundamentally broken. He replayed the moment endlessly, not as a clear memory, but as a searing feeling of failure. Why hadn't he seen the danger? What had he missed? This corrosive self-doubt began to poison his every decision. He started to believe he couldn't trust himself to do the right thing, whether it was choosing a delivery route or simply navigating a conversation with a stranger. This internal collapse was paired with a terrifying new conviction: the world itself was a malevolent and unpredictable place, a landscape of hidden threats where his old assumptions about decency and order no longer applied. Most frightening of all was the conclusion he drew from this new reality: if he were to truly let himself think about what happened, to feel the full weight of that helplessness again, he was certain he would not be able to handle it. He felt that the memory held the power to completely unmake him.

This set of beliefs—that he was untrustworthy, the world was hostile, and his own thoughts were a catastrophic threat—became the engine for a new way of living. To keep the memories and the terrifying feelings they produced at bay, Walter began to build a fortress of distraction. He started volunteering for the longest, most complex delivery routes, keeping himself on the road from before sunrise until long after his wife had eaten dinner alone. At home, the frantic activity continued. He would organize the garage, weed the garden in the dark, or disassemble and reassemble the lawnmower, anything to keep his hands and mind occupied. The silence was his enemy, the space where thoughts could creep in. When the anxiety still broke through, a raw and jittery feeling in his chest, he found a temporary solace in food. He started eating constantly throughout his day—stopping for donuts, burgers, anything to numb the feeling. In the quiet of the night, long after his wife was asleep, he would sit in the dim light of the kitchen and eat his way through a box of cookies or a bag of chips, a desperate attempt to push the dread back down.

His life became a grueling exercise in avoidance. He was running from his own mind, and the effort was exhausting him. The constant busyness created a chasm between him and his wife, who complained that he was a ghost in their own home. He had gained thirty pounds, and his doctor had expressed concern about his blood pressure. He knew his strategies weren't working, not really, but the alternative seemed so much worse. The breaking point came last week. A teenager on a skateboard shot out from between two parked cars, and Walter slammed on the brakes of his van, his heart seizing in his chest. For a moment, he wasn't on a busy street; he was back on that porch, helpless and on the ground. The panic was overwhelming, a tidal wave that his usual defenses could not hold back. He sat in his van for nearly an hour, shaking, unable to drive. It was the first time he truly understood that by refusing to look at the memory, he had given it complete control over his life. He came to the clinic the next day, his voice quiet and heavy with shame, admitting that he was terrified of talking about the trauma but even more terrified of what would happen if he didn't.
